transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Amy Held.
Despite scandals at NVIDIA, tech company stocks are climbing after a steep sell-off last month.
NPR's Stephen Bizaha reports the Nasdaq closed up about 2% for the week.
Big tech companies have a long way to go to recover from last month's artificial intelligence sell-off.
Chipmaker Intel's stock rose about 5.5% this week, but look back a month and its stock is still down more than 40%.
The biggest chipmaker in the market, NVIDIA, is still seeing its stock value fall, down about 12% this week.
After reports, it's now ousted CEO Jensen Wong had multiple affairs, including what the woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Now that drama is spilling into the upper ranks of the Trump administration.
Treasury Secretary Scott Beset blamed the Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for not restricting NVIDIA from selling its most advanced chips to China.
Stephen Bizaha, NPR News.
Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is calling for new leadership when Democrats become the new party in power in January.
He is running to replace Senator Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader after sweeping midterm wins.
The scale and scope of this victory, 56 Senate Democratic seats, really gives us a mandate and the votes to do big things.
But it should be very clear, while voters have rejected the Trump policies, they've not yet hired Democrats. They've given us a chance.
Van Hollen speaking to MS Now.
European leaders have agreed Germany, France, Italy, Poland and the UK will send diplomats to talks with the US, Russia and Ukraine.
Esmi Nicholson has this report.
Speaking after a summit focused on security and support for Ukraine, European Council President Antonio Costa said five of Europe's major military powers will join EU institutions at the table in US-led talks with Russia and Ukraine.
US envoy Jared Kushner and Ukrainian President Vladimir Zelensky said Thursday that Europe would be part of the next round of talks.
European leaders are concerned that Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold sway over the Trump administration to back a peace settlement that weakens Ukraine as well as Europe's security.
For NPR News, I'm Esmi Nicholson in Berlin.
In New Orleans, a tanker has struck a paddle-wheel cruise ship partially submerging the boat in the Mississippi River, officials say. More than 100 people were on board, their conditions unclear.
Some were seen in the water with life jackets on as rescues are underway.
A global Microsoft outage that sent businesses, governments, hospitals, schools and more into disarray yesterday is improving, the company says, but it warns of ongoing intermittent access issues.
Microsoft says an elevated load is behind the outage with no sign of malicious activity, but it says there is no ETA for full recovery. You're listening to NPR News.
Route 66 is turning 100 years old this year. The historic highway runs nearly 2,500 miles across eight states. NPR's Chloe Veltman reports it has long captured imaginations beyond the US.
According to a 2024 study conducted by the tourism research firm Smar Insights, international travellers are more likely to drive the entire length of Route 66 than those from within the United States.
Samir Patel is the manager of the Wigwam Motel, a popular stop on the highway in San Bernardino, California, where guests stay in concrete, TP-shaped guest rooms.
He says Route 66 has been popular for decades with Europeans as well as people from Australia and New Zealand.
And then lately, I would say the past four or five years, it's become very popular in South America, and then it's getting very popular in Asia as well.
Patel says on average 60-70% of the Wigwam's guests come from overseas, though he's seen an uptick in US visitors this year for the centennial. Chloe Veltman, NPR News.
SpaceX is hoping its 15th Starship launch makes history. Liftoff is set for next hour from Texas, but it's the ending that's really on the line, the aim, to catch the booster plus the spacecraft for the first time.
Elsewhere in the universe, next week a NASA robotic probe is set to reach one light day from Earth. That's the distance. A particle of light can travel in 24 hours, some 16 billion miles away farther than any man-made object has ever gone.
It was launched in 1977. Expected to last just five years, it's still going strong collecting data. It's NPR News.

topics.text: NVIDIA scandals weigh on chip stocks, though tech shares rebound modestly for the week
Former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's affairs spill into Trump administration as Bessent blames Lutnick
Senator Chris Van Hollen seeks Senate Majority Leader post after Democrats' midterm wins
European countries Germany, France, Italy, Poland and UK to join US-led Ukraine-Russia peace talks
Tanker strikes paddle-wheel cruise ship on Mississippi River in New Orleans, partially submerging it
Global Microsoft outage improving, with intermittent access problems continuing and no full-recovery estimate
Route 66 centennial draws growing international travelers, including at San Bernardino's Wigwam Motel
SpaceX launches 15th Starship test flight from Texas, aiming to catch booster and spacecraft
NASA's Voyager probe set to reach one light day from Earth, farther than any human-made object
